audit.reasoning: Source choice is right: the classification rests on Baart 1997, the fieldworker's phonology monograph, sec. 5.6 'Tone and word stress' p. 48 — the same page StressTyp2 cites — and no better description of Kalami stress exists in Glottolog's list or turned up in open repositories (SIL archive lists 1997, the 1999 sketch grammar and the 2008 OUP tones chapter as not online; BSOAS 1999 and Benjamins 2014 are paywalled). The classification 'lexical' (stress position depends on the word's lexical tonal melody: >80% final in isolation, all non-final-stress words = HL melody, position shifts with pitch jumps) is consistent across three channels I could check today: the StressTyp2 dump's own gloss of p. 48 ('Only words with HL melody may have other stress.. sources.quote: pp. 7-8: 'The most basic observation for all the tone languages of northern Pakistan is that the tone features are associated with the stressed syllable. The pitch patterns that are characteristic of one tone or another, occur on or near the stressed syllable.' p. 11: 'Kalami-type languages have four distinctive pitch patterns on the surface ... (Kalami itself has in fact two types of falling pitch patterns ...) ... we must assume that both H and L can occur in the underlying forms. (For an analysis of Kalami tone, see Baart 1997: 40-49 and 1999.)' No statement of where Kalami word stress fall
